tldr: We present HyperDrone, a simulator that completely integrates hardware-accelerated ray tracing and drone dynamics on the GPU to achieve rendering speeds of millions of frames per second. A vision-based yaw-control policy trained purely on synthetic images was successfully transferred zero-shot to an onboard NPU of a real small-scale drone.
hero_caption: Overall system architecture of HyperDrone. Multirotor dynamics simulation, HyperLux ray-tracing rendering, the teacher policy (RAPTOR), and the student policy being trained all reside entirely within a single GPU's memory, completely eliminating host-device transfer bottlenecks.
overview:
In recent years, imitation learning from real-world robot data has attracted significant attention, but for aerial robots, the cost of large-scale real data collection and poor reproducibility have posed serious barriers. Reinforcement learning inside physics simulators offers a promising alternative. However, training vision-based control policies directly from image inputs requires both physics simulation and massive camera rendering to run at extreme speeds.

Conventional drone simulators have suffered from graphics rendering bottlenecks, reaching throughputs of only a few hundred to tens of thousands of FPS. Furthermore, they face challenges such as data transfer overhead between the CPU and GPU, as well as a lack of support for modern GPU architectures. To address these issues, this study developed "HyperLux," a new rendering engine that fully utilizes the dedicated ray-tracing hardware (RT Cores) of modern GPUs, and integrated it with multirotor dynamics on the exact same GPU to create "HyperDrone."

This system achieves extraordinary batch-rendering performance of millions of frames per second (FPS) even on consumer-grade GPUs. Furthermore, using 10,000 diverse indoor scenes (ProcTHOR), the authors trained a vision-based yaw-control policy and deployed it onto the camera and NPU mounted on a micro quadrotor (Crazyflie). Flight experiments in a real environment demonstrated that the model trained solely on synthetic images without any real-world data could accurately track the target yaw orientation on the real drone.
contributions: Built the ray-tracing engine HyperLux to directly leverage RT Cores on modern GPUs, achieving rendering performance of millions of frames per second—more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators.
Ran dynamics, ray-tracing rendering, and policy network inference and training entirely on a single GPU, completely eliminating memory transfer latency between the CPU and GPU.

Realized a flexible rendering pipeline capable of reproducing reflections, Physically Based Rendering (PBR), anti-aliasing, and physics-based motion blur with high fidelity and low computational overhead.

Trained a vision-based yaw-estimation policy from scratch purely on synthetic images in simulation and deployed it to an onboard NPU of a real small-scale drone (Crazyflie), demonstrating Sim2Real transfer.

sections.heading: Limits of Real-World Data Collection and the Need for Pure Simulation
sections.summary: In autonomous aerial robotics, the cost and monopolization of real-world data collection severely compromise research reproducibility. This section discusses the importance of learning purely from transparent and reproducible synthetic data, and the motivation behind HyperDrone to break through the rendering speed barrier that previously hindered it.
sections.details:
In manipulation and quadrupedal robotics, imitation learning using human teleoperation demonstrations and the introduction of vision foundation models pretrained on web images have progressed rapidly. However, scaling the same approach to aerial robots like drones is far from easy.

Data collection in the real world requires massive capital expenditure (CAPEX). When a few well-funded corporate entities monopolize data, it undermines reproducibility across the research community. Moreover, the training datasets for pretrained models are often private, making it difficult to inspect black-box behaviors.

In contrast, training policies entirely within a physics simulator allows every aspect of the data generation process to be scrutinized, guaranteeing experimental reproducibility. However, end-to-end image-based learning requires millions to billions of frames, and conventional simulators render far too slowly, resulting in excessive training times. The authors therefore propose "HyperDrone," an extremely fast quadrotor simulator designed to unlock the maximum potential of modern hardware.

sections.heading: The Rendering Bottleneck Faced by Existing Simulators
sections.summary: This section summarizes the strengths and weaknesses of existing drone simulators such as Flightmare, Isaac Gym, and Habitat-based VisFly. It highlights why many current tools fail to fully leverage modern dedicated GPU hardware, limiting both rendering realism and speed.
sections.details:
Flightmare, a widely used simulator for aerial robotics, lacks batch-rendering support and achieves a low throughput of roughly 230 FPS, which is insufficient to supply the volume of data needed for reinforcement learning. Modifying or importing scenes also requires commercial software.

Recently, simulators that introduce batch rendering for acceleration have emerged. For example, VisFly is based on Habitat (OpenGL/Magnum) and supports Nvidia's latest Blackwell generation (RTX 5000 series), but it falls short in visual fidelities critical for real-world transfer, such as motion blur and anti-aliasing.

Furthermore, Aerial Gym, which is based on Isaac Gym, specializes in depth and segmentation and cannot render RGB images on arbitrary 3D meshes. With the end-of-life of Isaac Gym, support for newer GPU architectures has also ended. OmniDrones, based on Isaac Sim, has similarly ceased maintenance, raising concerns about future compatibility. In addition, adopting Madrona, a fast ray tracer, was evaluated; however, because it does not utilize RTX RT Cores and presents codebase complexity, the authors opted to build an entirely new engine tailored for this research.

sections.heading: HyperLux Directly on RT Cores: A Fully GPU-Contained Pipeline
sections.summary: This section details the internal architecture of HyperDrone and the Sim2Real transfer pipeline from synthetic images to a physical drone. Key elements include a design eliminating CPU-GPU transfers, the adoption of open glTF 2.0 standards, and a probe ray spatial sampling method.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Architecture
The defining feature of HyperDrone is that quadrotor dynamics, ray-tracing rendering (HyperLux), and policy network training and inference are all contained entirely inside the GPU. In conventional simulators, physics is computed on the CPU and states are sent to the GPU for rendering, creating a bus transfer bottleneck; by utilizing the OptiX backend, HyperDrone completely eliminates memory copies.

The rendering engine HyperLux relies on ray tracing rather than rasterization (projecting polygons onto the screen). To directly exploit the RT Cores (fixed-function hardware dedicated to ray-mesh intersection tests) on modern GPUs, it supports OptiX, Vulkan, and Metal, with WebGPU provided as a fallback. Because rendering performance is so high, images do not need to be cached or reused during training; newly rendered frames are continuously generated in real time, fundamentally preventing overfitting.

### 3.2 Visual Sim2Real Transfer Setup
To validate visual Sim2Real transfer, the research team intentionally constrained the degrees of freedom to a relative yaw angle estimation task using vision. For low-level position control and attitude stabilization, they used a pretrained teacher policy, "RAPTOR," which outputs direct motor commands at 500 Hz. The student network to be trained is a compact CNN that takes two channel-concatenated images—the target image and the current image—and predicts the relative yaw angle between them.

The training environment leverages 10,000 procedurally generated indoor scenes from the "ProcTHOR" dataset. Using the open standard glTF 2.0 (.glb) makes asset sharing and extension straightforward. To safely determine initial spawn locations within scenes, the system casts 64 "probe rays" in a spherical Fibonacci spiral from the drone position and performs fast rejection sampling to ensure at least 1 m clearance from obstacles and walls. For the real-world platform, a Crazyflie quadrotor is used, executing the trained CNN on the onboard NPU of an OpenMV AE3 camera board.

captions.F3: Control architecture deployed on the real drone (Crazyflie). The student CNN runs on the NPU of the OpenMV AE3 camera board, estimating the relative yaw angle between the current and target images, and transmits setpoints via UART to the low-level attitude controller (RAPTOR) running on the microcontroller.
captions.F5: A ProcTHOR indoor scene (left) and the probe ray configuration used for spawn location sampling (right). By casting 64 rays in a Fibonacci sphere from the drone's position to evaluate surrounding clearance, RT Core acceleration keeps the computational overhead to only about 1.6%.

sections.heading: Millions of Frames Per Second and Real-World Onboard Deployment
sections.summary: This section reports visual fidelity comparisons, throughput benchmarks drastically outperforming existing tools, and visual yaw-tracking experiments on a real micro drone. With only a few hours of training, the drone achieved smooth real-world yaw-tracking flight.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Visual Fidelity Evaluation
HyperLux offers three rendering modes depending on the application: High, Medium, and Low. In High mode, it faithfully represents PBR materials, point and spot lights, and planar specular reflections on table surfaces. It also supports depth, segmentation, surface normals, and optical flow observations commonly used in robot learning. To address jaggies (aliasing) in low-resolution rendering (e.g., $64\times 64$), anti-aliasing averages $2\times 2$ rays per pixel, reducing the Sim2Real gap. In addition, motion blur during rapid rotations can be physically simulated by subsampling over the shutter duration; experiments showed that setting 2 samples is sufficient for real-world transfer.

### 4.2 Rendering and Simulation Throughput
In benchmark measurements on an RTX 4090 (16GB, capped at 80W), HyperDrone recorded more than $20\times$ higher throughput than existing state-of-the-art batch drone simulators (such as VisFly). Even in High mode (RGB) within ProcTHOR scenes, performance remained dominant, delivering extraordinary speeds across varied hardware, including an RTX 5090 and a Mac Studio (approx. 1.5 million FPS under Metal). Compared to the fast renderer Madrona, HyperDrone maintained more than a $5\times$ throughput advantage at comparable visual fidelity.

### 4.3 Successful Sim2Real Transfer
Training the vision-based yaw-control network completed in just 4 hours on an RTX 5090 (consuming roughly 6 GB of GPU memory, and trainable on an RTX 3060 in about 15 hours). The reinforcement learning framework utilizes RLtools, ensuring fully deterministic execution (fixing the seed produces bit-identical results) across the entire pipeline, including the simulator. When deployed on the real Crazyflie, the policy relied on real-world visual features—such as chairs and step ladders in the room—to accurately track alternating yaw commands between two target images.

captions.F6: Image quality comparison across rendering modes (High / Medium / Low / Depth), resolutions ($2048\times 2048$ down to $64\times 64$), and anti-aliasing (with/without 4xAA). Applying AA dramatically reduces edge aliasing even at low resolutions.
captions.F7: Simulation comparison of motion blur during drone rotation. Shutter time (vertical axis) and ray subsample count (horizontal axis) are varied; physically integrating multiple rays over time captures natural blur without relying on game-engine approximations.
captions.F8: Experimental results of target image tracking with the physical drone. For two distinct target images (bottom), the drone's real yaw angle (blue line) smoothly and accurately tracks the reference setpoint (red dashed line).

sections.heading: Future Challenges: Rolling Shutter Support and Autonomous Collision Avoidance
sections.summary: This section summarizes the current limitations of HyperDrone and planned future extensions. Key avenues include handling rolling shutter artifacts and expanding to higher-frequency, full end-to-end control tasks.
sections.details:
Despite showing dramatic speedups and successful Sim2Real transfer, HyperDrone has several clear limitations:

- No rolling shutter support: The camera model currently assumes a global shutter. Simulating the rolling shutter distortion common in low-cost CMOS sensors remains future work.
- Unintegrated collision avoidance: While probe rays are implemented for spatial spawn sampling, testing them as a continuous collision checking and obstacle avoidance interface during active flight has not yet been conducted.
- Simplified control task: The real-world demonstration was limited to low-frequency yaw control relying on external localization and a pretrained controller (RAPTOR). Expanding to full end-to-end control for high-speed agile flight and dynamic obstacle avoidance is needed.

The authors plan to address these challenges while providing the codebase to the community as an openly maintained foundation.

sections.heading: Democratizing Vision-Based Drone Control Research for Everyone
sections.summary: This section summarizes HyperDrone's impact on the research community. By enabling ultrafast vision learning on consumer GPUs, it significantly accelerates the democratization of autonomous aerial robotics research.
sections.details:
By fully taking advantage of modern GPU hardware characteristics, HyperDrone achieves an order-of-magnitude leap in drone visual simulation speeds. In contrast to research paradigms reliant on expensive real-world data collection, this work demonstrates a viable path toward training capable policies purely from synthetic data and physics simulation.

Because development cycles can be dramatically shortened on standard consumer hardware without requiring costly compute clusters, HyperDrone serves as a powerful tool for academic researchers and independent developers alike. The research team intends to maintain an open, extensible ecosystem to advance the fully autonomous flight stack together with the community.

sections.heading: Appendix: Dynamics Model, Shading Details, and Curriculum Learning
sections.summary: This appendix covers technical specifics regarding multirotor equations of motion, PBR material shading in HyperLux, and the curriculum training pipeline for the student network.
sections.details:
### Dynamics Model
Multirotor dynamics are modeled using state equations with position $\mathbf{p}$, quaternion $\mathbf{q}$, velocity $\mathbf{v}$, angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$, and motor speed $\boldsymbol{\omega}_m$. The thrust $f_i$ for each motor is computed as a quadratic polynomial of its rotational speed, accounting for a first-order motor lag time constant $T_{m_i}$ as well as random disturbance forces and torques.

### Shading Specifications of Fidelity Modes
HyperLux's three fidelity modes are toggled via compile-time flags, meaning disabled features incur zero runtime cost. Low mode uses flat colors baked from the average texture color at load time; Medium mode adds view-dependent attenuation and single-bounce specular reflections on metallic surfaces; High mode fully adheres to the glTF 2.0 PBR standard, calculating normal maps, roughness/metallic maps, ProcTHOR point lights, and ambient reflection rays.

### Student Model Training Pipeline
Out of 30 ProcTHOR training scenes, 25 are used for training and 5 for validation. Simulating 128 parallel environments per epoch, curriculum learning gradually expands the initial orientation offset angle $\theta_{\mathrm{max}}$ from $0^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$. The student network comprises 4 convolutional layers (32 to 256 channels) and 3 fully connected layers with approximately 730k parameters, with input channels padded to 8 to match the OpenMV onboard NPU constraints.

takeaways: Directly utilizing dedicated GPU RT Cores boosts visual simulation throughput by more than 20x compared to existing simulators (reaching millions of FPS), eliminating the reinforcement learning bottleneck.
Unifying dynamics, ray tracing, and policy training on the same GPU memory removes CPU-GPU transfer latency and avoids overfitting by generating fresh frames on the fly without sample reuse.
Incorporating physically grounded anti-aliasing and motion blur allows a vision policy trained purely on synthetic images to transfer zero-shot (Sim2Real) to a physical micro drone.
Adopting open 3D standards like glTF 2.0 alongside procedural datasets like ProcTHOR enables anyone to build reproducible, highly diverse training environments.
limitations: Rolling shutter artifacts typical of micro CMOS cameras are not yet modeled, as the simulator currently assumes a global shutter.

Although probe rays are used for spatial clearance checks, active 3D mesh collision detection and reactive obstacle avoidance algorithms during high-speed real flight remain unintegrated and unvalidated.
The Sim2Real demonstration was restricted to visual yaw setpoint tracking, leaving full end-to-end control—including position tracking and aggressive aerobatics—as future work.
